summary:
The Riau Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The country overview records the same provision as carrying up to one year's imprisonment when a complaint is lodged.

Two provinces of Indonesia, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Neither province is the Riau Islands, and no source in this inventory records equivalent provincial criminalisation here.

Enforcement elsewhere in Indonesia takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled, listing "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" alongside terrorism and drug addiction. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks: in July 2026 mobs attacked transgender women in several cities including West Java, with no prosecutions reported, and civil society describes rapidly worsening conditions. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

For the Riau Islands specifically, the inventory records no province-specific divergence from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02), and no unit-specific findings. Private same-sex conduct is not criminalised nationally but attracts no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, and legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. A 2020 raid case documented in the country overview shows how enforcement varies with local bylaws: those held were released because no regional regulation existed.
tangentialFactors:
Indonesia's diplomatic posture is documented: the state voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025, and no national anti-discrimination instrument covering gender identity is recorded.

Public attitudes are strongly hostile. Pew recorded 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality morally unacceptable in 2025 and 95% opposition to same-sex marriage in 2023. These figures are national and are not disaggregated for the Riau Islands.

The enforcement picture is uneven across Indonesia. Aceh's caning sentence of February 2025 and the Puncak villa raid of June 2025 show religious-law and morality-based enforcement in other provinces, while the 2020 raid release shows detainees going free where no regional regulation exists. The Riau Islands sits in the second category on the evidence available: no provincial criminalisation of same-sex conduct is sourced here, but neither is any provincial protection.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Riau Islands live under the national penal code in force from 2 January 2026, under which a complaint about consensual extra-marital sex can lead to imprisonment, and under national morality provisions that have been used against LGBTQ+ people elsewhere in the country.

Legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery and judicial approval. There is no recorded pathway allowing recognition on the basis of identity alone, and no source in this inventory records a province-specific procedure or a shorter timeline for the Riau Islands.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or hate crime on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation, and the October 2025 presidential decree places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as a nonmilitary threat to be monitored and controlled.

Local bylaws matter in practice: where a regional regulation against same-sex conduct does not exist, those detained in a raid have been released. The inventory does not record a regional regulation of that kind for the Riau Islands.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory is specific to the Riau Islands. The province-level position rests on the absence of recorded divergence from the national framework, which is an absence of evidence rather than a positive finding of safety, and no local reporting on raids, arrests or venue closures in this province was available.

The penalty for extra-marital sex is stated inconsistently across the supplied material: the national framework text gives up to two years' imprisonment, while the country overview gives up to one year when a complaint is lodged. This discrepancy is unresolved and should be checked against the text of the amended penal code.

Whether the 2020 raid release occurred in the Riau Islands or elsewhere in Indonesia is not sourced here; it is cited only as evidence that enforcement turns on the existence of a regional regulation.

Entry, visa and airport-screening treatment of trans travellers arriving in the Riau Islands, the availability of gender-affirming care locally, and the presence or absence of LGBTQ+ venues in this province are not covered by the inventory and remain unresolved.

The July 2026 mob attacks are reported at national level with West Java named; no source attributes attacks, threats or vigilante activity to the Riau Islands.
